t: he shall leave some standing grain. He shall leave a few stalks attached to the ground.
for the poor. For the definition of a poor person see below 9:13.
whether one who reaps or one who plucks. One who reaps with a tool and one who plucks by hand.
you shall leave. You shall leave and set aside.

for he violated a negative commandment etc.. It is a rule that one is not flogged for a negative commandment accompanied by a positive commandment to be performed if one transgressed the negative (a "negative commandment that is resolved by a positive one," see Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:2). But when it is impossible to fulfill the positive commandment, one is flogged for the negative (there; for further examples see also Hilchot Na'arah Betulah 1:7, 3:4, Hilchot Shechitah 13:1-2, Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 3:4).
and binds sheaves. Gathers stalks into a bundle.
even if he ground and baked, he gives the poor. Part of the flour or bread.
and likewise with the peret that falls from grapes. One or two grapes that fell from the cluster during the harvest, which it is forbidden to gather as gleanings.
and likewise with olelot. Small clusters given to the poor (for their definition see below 4:17).
you shall not glean. You shall not take the olelot.
one who gathers into sheaves. Collects cut stalks and ties them together.
a sheaf. A bundle of stalks.
when you beat your olive tree, you shall not go over the boughs again. When you strike the branches so that they drop their fruit, you shall not go back and gather what remains on the branches.
the owners have no benefit of giving. The owners have no right to profit from choosing which poor person they give to (see also below 6:10).
even a poor person in Israel. Even if the owner of the field is poor, he is obligated to give the gifts to the poor.

every convert mentioned in the gifts to the poor. In the Torah verses dealing with gifts to the poor (and the reference is to converts who are poor, as is evident from the verse, "for the poor and for the stranger you shall leave them" - Leviticus 19:10).

a righteous convert. A gentile who converted and accepted all the commandments of the Torah, whose law is like that of a Jew (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 12:17; for the process of his conversion see there 14:1-6).
a member of the covenant. A Jew.
one does not prevent poor gentiles from these gifts etc.. See also Hilchot Avodah Zarah 10:5; and similarly below 4:13, 7:7.
the poor stopped seeking and returning to them. Searching for them in the field.

for their body is not holy like terumot. Unlike terumah, which is holy and permitted for eating only to a kohen, the gifts to the poor have no sanctity and are therefore permitted for eating even to one who is not poor.
and he is not obligated to give them their value. To pay the worth of the gifts to the poor (unlike the priestly gifts, compare Hilchot Bikkurim 9:16).

after the poor have walked through the vineyard and entered. For it is the way of the poor person to comb through the field twice: when entering the field, and on his way out (Shenot Eliyahu, Pe'ah 8:1).

at the top of the olive tree, it is permitted from the new moon of Kislev. Until then is the proper time for picking olives, and after that the poor will not bother with the olives remaining in the tree.
the second rainfall. The second rainy season.
in a dark year. In a year when winter comes late.

as long as the poor person has etc.. As long as the poor person is still searching for the olives beneath the tree, he has the right to take them and it is forbidden for one who is not poor to take them, even though the new moon of Kislev has arrived, when olives forgotten at the top of the tree become permitted to everyone.

and as long as he has etc.. Before the new moon of Kislev the poor person has the right to take olives forgotten at the top of the tree, even if no olives were forgotten beneath the tree (according to Kesef Mishneh; for other interpretations see Derech Emunah and Yad Peshutah).
for the poor are not particular about them. For example, because of the small quantity or an unimportant kind.
like terumot and ma'aserot. See Hilchot Terumot 1:1.
by rabbinic decree. By the words of the Sages.
whose growth is from the earth. That has roots in the ground (unlike mushrooms, as explained in the next halachah).
and is guarded. That it is guarded and is not ownerless growth, nor a kind that people are not particular about.
and its harvest is all at once. All its fruit ripens at the same time.
and is brought in for storage. That it is stored for some time and does not rot or dry out immediately.
fresh. Moist.
isatis and puah. Plants used to make dye.
truffles. A kind of fungus.
whose growth is not from the earth like other produce of the earth. They have no roots and do not draw nourishment from the soil like other plants.
what will ripen today. What will ripen today.
the greens. For example, leafy vegetables that do not keep for long.
the mother bulbs of onions etc.. Onions that are not harvested and are left in the ground to grow new onions.
and any amount of land. Even very small.

a field that gentiles harvested for themselves. For example, they intended to steal the harvest and ultimately left the grain in the field (but if they harvested on behalf of the owner it is obligated in pe'ah, as below, halachah 10).
ants gnawed it. They gnawed and ate the stalks and the grain became detached from the ground.

for the obligation of pe'ah applies to standing grain. The obligation to leave pe'ah applies when one harvests grain standing in the field ("bakomah" - while standing), and since it was not obligated in pe'ah then, it is no longer obligated.
for the obligation applies to the half that the bandits harvested. Since the obligation of pe'ah applies only at the end of the harvest, see below, halachah 12.
to the amount he harvested. Only in the amount needed for what he harvested, since harvesting by bandits is exempt from pe'ah.
the buyer gives pe'ah for all. The buyer gives pe'ah in the amount required for the entire field, since the obligation of pe'ah is at the end of the harvest.
one who redeems from the treasurer. One who buys the field from the treasurer of the Temple.
he harvested half of it and consecrated it. And he harvested the other half for himself.
and he intends to leave the rest for the winepress to tread it. He intends to postpone harvesting the remaining grapes in order to make wine from them.

if he was harvesting for the market from here and from there etc.. If he harvested a little from each side, then when he leaves pe'ah on what he harvests for the winepress, he need not leave pe'ah on what he already harvested, since harvesting in this way is a casual harvest, and is exempt from pe'ah.

and if he was harvesting for the market from one side only etc.. If he harvested from one place only, he must leave pe'ah for the entire field, for the first harvest is not considered a casual harvest (and see below 3:23).
one who plucks ears little by little and brings them into his house. Plucks a few ears each time, and is exempt because this is an incidental harvest.
before it is finished. Before it ripens.
it has not reached a third. It has not reached a third of its growth.
it is exempt. For it is not yet fruit (Rik"v; and see also Hilchot Terumot 2:10, regarding exemption from terumah and tithes).
and it is standing. When it has grain attached to the ground.

for at the time of the obligation of pe'ah it was consecrated property, which is not obligated in pe'ah. At the time of harvest it was in the hands of the Temple treasury, and consecrated property is exempt from pe'ah (see also Hilchot Ma'aser 2:8, Hilchot Bikkurim 8:7).

even though forgotten sheaves apply only at the time of binding. And at that time he was already a convert, he is nevertheless exempt from forgotten sheaves, for only what became obligated while standing in leket and pe'ah becomes obligated at the time of binding in forgotten sheaves (Commentary on the Mishnah, Pe'ah 4:6).
because they are not expert in leket and pe'ah. They are not expert in how they should be given.
who harvested his whole field etc.. See above 1:2.
and he does not need to tithe. By the law of pe'ah, which is exempt from terumot and ma'aserot (Hilchot Terumot 2:9).
and even if he gave them most of the harvest as pe'ah. For one may add to the amount of pe'ah (above 1:15).

he threshed and has not yet winnowed. The act of threshing separates the grain from its husks, but the husks are still mixed with the grain, and the act of winnowing in the wind removes the husks from the mixture.
with a winnowing fork and a shovel. Winnowing implements.
and finished his work. The final action in the process of working the crop is called "completion of work," and from then it is obligated in tithes (Hilchot Ma'aser 3:1).

he tithes and afterward gives them. For the crop is already obligated in tithes, and he may not tithe at the expense of the poor, since gifts to the poor would have been exempt from tithes had the owner given them on time; therefore he tithes first and then gives the poor their share in full.
and so that he not be suspected. Of not having left pe'ah.
that he not wait for a time etc.. That he not wait for a time when no other poor are there, and give it to the poor person he wants.
the amount of pe'ah appropriate for what remained in the field after he separated the first. In the amount appropriate for the quantity he harvested after giving the first pe'ah.
both are pe'ah. Since he designated them as pe'ah, both became pe'ah, for he may give more pe'ah than the required amount, as above, halachah 11 (Radbaz).
and the poor have no claim to it etc.. Although the laborers left pe'ah in the field, it is forbidden for the poor to take it before the owner designates it as pe'ah.
and the poor plunder it. They take as much as they can.
if those poor wanted to divide it among themselves. Equally.
for he said according to the halachah. According to the essential law.
a trellised vine. A vine trained upward.
except with great danger. They would push one another and fall from a great height.
and divides among the poor. Equally.
and if they all wanted to plunder it. If they agreed among themselves that each would grab as much as he can.
they divide the pe'ah among the poor in the field. For trellised vines and date palms.
or they leave them to plunder it. For other kinds.
and at Minchah. The time of minchah ketanah, at nine and a half seasonal hours.

so that there will be a fixed time for the poor to gather and all take. So that it will not happen that the owner invites only his poor relatives to take, at a time when no other poor are present (as above, halachah 12, Rosh, Pe'ah 4:5).
young poor people. Youths.
a poor person who took part of the pe'ah and threw it over the rest. In order to hide the pe'ah so that other poor will not take it (Commentary on the Mishnah, Pe'ah 4:3).
and even what he took, one takes from his hand. Even the pe'ah he threw in order to conceal, though he already acquired it (Derech Emunah).
since he acquired it for himself, he acquired it for that person. Since he can take it for himself, he can acquire it for his poor friend.

and if he is wealthy he did not acquire for him etc.. For he has no right to take it for himself, and he also cannot acquire it on behalf of another, because one cannot acquire on behalf of others if there are other rightful claimants in the very same item (see also Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 20:2).
who left pe'ah for these poor people standing before him. It is possible for them to take it, but they have not yet taken it.
and a sela found as a lost item. A coin he found.
until they reach his hand. Until he grasps them in his hand (see also Hilchot Gezelah VaAvedah 17:1).
pe'ah appropriate for both. In the amount needed for both fields.
you shall not complete the corner of your field when you reap. From the word "your field" we learn that pe'ah must be left in each field separately.
it is not pe'ah. And he must separate additional pe'ah on the second field.
that does not flow. In which water is not currently flowing.
a water channel from which he cannot reap both its sides at once. A water channel where, standing on one side, one cannot harvest the stalks on the other side (Commentary on the Mishnah, Pe'ah 2:2).
flowing and fixed. In which water flows constantly.
a private path. One made for the walking of an individual.
fixed in the summer days and the rainy days. That people walk on it in all seasons of the year.
even before it reached a third and he plowed the place he harvested. Even though he harvested the grain at an early stage, this is not a separation unless the area was plowed (Kesef Mishneh).
like three furrows of a petiach. The width of three furrows of a plow (Commentary on the Mishnah, Pe'ah 2:1), the measure of a width of two cubits (Pe'at HaShulchan 6:5).
and it is less than a beit rova. The measure of three furrows of a petiach is less than the width of a beit rova mentioned shortly.
fifty cubits by two cubits. A long, narrow field whose area is slightly smaller than a beit rova.

but if it was larger than this etc.. If the field is larger than this, only fallow or plowed land of the width of a beit rova constitutes a separation, for since the field is large a smaller break is not noticeable in it.
the width of a beit rova. Slightly more than ten cubits wide (Rash Sirilio, Pe'ah 2:1), for a beit rova is ten and a fifth cubits by ten and a fifth cubits (see Hilchot Kilayim 3:9).

but any amount of another seed divides it. For in a large field it is not customary to sow two kinds, and therefore another seed is noticeable even in a small quantity; unlike a small field in which it is customary to sow more than one kind, so another seed divides it only at a width of about two cubits, as above (Radbaz and Rik"v).
a gubai. A type of locust.
hills upon hills that are high and places upon places that are deep. It has high places and low places.

even though he cannot etc.. Although the sowing and plowing of these places is done separately because of the differences in height, they are considered one field because ultimately the whole field is sown continuously (Commentary on the Mishnah, Pe'ah 2:2).
terraces that are ten handbreadths high. A field sown on a mountain slope in terraced fashion, each row ten handbreadths higher than the one below it.
the heads of the rows are mixed. The beginnings of the rows are joined to one another.
if there was a rock across the entire field. A rocky strip that crosses the field from end to end.
if he lifts the plow from this side and places it on that side. If he must lift the plow to move it to the other side.
rectangles upon rectangles between the trees. The field is sown in square plots separated from each other by the trees between them.
every ten within a beit se'ah. A density of at least ten trees in an area not exceeding a beit se'ah (an area of fifty cubits by fifty cubits).
the onion plots among the greens. Square onion beds scattered among the vegetable beds.

and even though the greens separate between them etc.. And the vegetables are not treated as another seed that divides (above, halachah 4), because this is how onions are customarily sown, in small beds between vegetable beds (Aruch HaShulchan, Pe'ah 6:6).
to dry. To ripen.
until the moist part remained separated, in plots distant from one another. The part that had not ripened remained in separate beds.
dill. Dill.
in what case does this apply?. That he gives one pe'ah for all.

dry from here and dry from there and moist in the middle. That he harvested from the sides of the field and the center of the field remained. Since the bulk of the field remained, he separates one pe'ah for all (Radbaz, and see other interpretations in Kesef Mishneh, Rik"v, and Derech Emunah).
moist from here and from there and dry in the middle. That he harvested from the middle of the field, and a bare patch was created there.
he leaves from the dry by itself and from the moist by itself. For the bare patch divides, and therefore he separates from the dry by itself, and from each bed of the moist by itself (Kesef Mishneh).
and he intended to sell etc.. His intention is to pick part of the crop and sell it fresh, and leave the rest in the field until it dries and then gather it.
for the market and the threshing floor are like two kinds. For the moist is eaten as is, and the dry requires processing such as grinding or cooking, and they are like different kinds (Yad Peshutah).
two threshing floors. He harvests the field at two different times.
one threshing floor. He harvests them together.
varieties. Strains.
a law given to Moses at Sinai. A halachic tradition.
brothers who divided. They received a field as inheritance from their father and divided it among themselves before the harvest.
they returned and became partners. After dividing, they made a partnership in the field before it was harvested (Vilna Gaon).
partners who harvested half the field and afterward divided. They harvested half of it as partners, and then dissolved the partnership.

this one who took the harvested part etc. and this one who took the standing part etc.. The one who received the part already harvested is exempt from giving pe'ah, for at the time of harvest he was not yet obligated, since the obligation applies only at the end of the harvest (Kesef Mishneh), and the other, who received the part not yet harvested ("the standing grain"), must separate pe'ah only on his own portion, and need not separate on his fellow's portion.

they returned and became partners and harvested the other half in partnership, each of them separates etc.. If both of them renewed the partnership and only then harvested the other half, they may give pe'ah together by the law of partners. However, only the half of the field that remained to be harvested is obligated in pe'ah. The half of the field harvested before the dissolution of the partnership remains exempt from pe'ah.

a field half of which reached a third etc.. A field half of which reached a third of its ripening (only then is it obligated in pe'ah, above 2:7), and he harvested half of this part (a quarter of the crop), and after the other half reached a third of its ripening, he finished harvesting the first half.

he separates from the first for the middle ones etc.. He may separate pe'ah from the first quarter he harvested for the second quarter (the "middle ones"), and vice versa, since both reached a third before the harvest of the first. And likewise he may separate from the second quarter for the second half of the field, since the second quarter was harvested only after the second half reached a third.

but not from the first for the last. He cannot separate from the first quarter for the last half, and vice versa, since one cannot separate pe'ah from produce harvested at the beginning for produce that was not yet obligated in pe'ah at the time the first produce was harvested.
a high fence that separates the trees. At least ten handbreadths high (Commentary on the Mishnah, Pe'ah 2:3).
and the branches and the boughs. The thick and thin branches of the two trees.
intertwined above and touching the fence on top of it. Extending over the fence and tangled with one another.

the carob trees. Carob trees have a different law from other trees, and a fence does not divide among them because of their height (Ra'avad in his glosses), or because it is customary to plant them far from one another (Sefer Yereim, commandment 119).
but he may not separate from the first side for the other side. He cannot separate from the farthest carob tree for the carob tree on the other side, since they do not see one another.

the olives. Olives have a different law, because these trees are very common in the Land of Israel and the Sages did not want to burden people to give many pe'ot from them (Radbaz). Or because it was customary to build olive presses on the four sides of the city, they ordained that one gives one pe'ah for all the olives brought to each press (Jerusalem Talmud, Pe'ah 2:4).
to ease from the vine until the other clusters find room and grow. To give the clusters space in which they can grow.
and we have already explained. Above 2:6.
that one who harvests from one side is not a thinner. He is not considered a thinner but the start of the harvest.
but if he thinned to sell in the market, he does not give pe'ah for what he thinned. Since this is a casual harvest (see there).

if he thinned to bring to his house etc.. For example, one who treads the grapes and makes wine from them (Radbaz), or makes raisins from them (according to Rik"v). In this case what he thinned is obligated in pe'ah since it is evident that it is not a casual harvest.
and what falls from behind the sickle or from behind the hand. The stalks that were on the back of the sickle or outside the grasp of his hand.
if he was harvesting by hand. He plucks by hand something that is usually harvested with a sickle.
a thorn struck him. His hand was pricked by a thorn.
if its head reached the standing grain beside it. If it can be bent and harvested together with the standing grain.
and if not, it belongs to the poor. For its law is leket, even though it is attached (as explained in the next halachah).

the inner is saved and saves the outer. The first stalk can be harvested with the standing grain, and so it is not leket ("is saved"), and since the second stalk can be harvested with it, it too is not leket.

for it is like one that falls from the sickle, even though it has not yet been harvested. This explains why the outer stalk needs saving: since it was not harvested with the stalks around it, it is considered as if it fell from the sickle even though it is still attached.

and the stalks in the straw belong to the owner of the field. It seems to be explained that this refers to stalks found among the stubble (the stalks that remained attached to the ground after harvest), and we do not worry that these stalks are leket, but assume that the owner left them intentionally because of the effort (Derech Emunah, and see Yad Peshutah and Tosefta Kifshutah, end of Pe'ah chapter 2).
they estimate how much leket it should produce. They estimate what quantity of stalks would be expected to fall in a field of this size.
because this is beyond his control. And therefore he was not penalized, as in the next halachot.
four kavs. About 4.8 liters.
for every beit kor. An area suitable for sowing a kor of barley (75,000 square cubits).
and made a heap. Made a pile.
one who needs to water his field. To sprinkle a large quantity of water on it, and the leket lying in it might rot.
and if he gathered all the leket etc.. In a case where they permitted him to water.
in ant holes. In the holes of ants, in their burrows.
within the standing grain. In the area not yet harvested.

and even though it was found black etc.. At the time of harvest the grain is light, since it dried for a long time. By contrast, after a period buried in the ground its color becomes dark. If black kernels are found in ant holes, we do not say that they are from last year and the poor have already despaired of them, but we are concerned that perhaps they are from this harvest and have the law of leket, for sometimes there are also black kernels in harvested grain, and a doubt about leket is treated as leket (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Pe'ah 4:11).

he separates two stalks and says etc.. One cannot give the poor person an unspecified stalk, for leket is exempt from tithes while the rest of the heap is obligated, and if he is given a stalk from which he must tithe, he has not received what is due to him; therefore the stalk given to the poor must be tithed (regarding the need for a double condition and its various details, see the commentators on the Rambam, especially Yad Peshutah, Derech Emunah, and Aruch HaShulchan 8:17).

a person may not hire a worker on condition that his son glean after him. For he is robbing the poor (Jerusalem Talmud, Pe'ah 5:5, Commentary on the Mishnah, Pe'ah 5:6), for example in a case where the worker's son drives away other poor people (Ein Yosef, Bava Metzia 12a), or where the owner reduced the worker's wages because of the leket his son gleans, so that the owner profits from the leket (Rash, Pe'ah 5:6, Radbaz).
but sharecroppers etc.. In these cases there was no condition, and therefore his son may glean after him.
and one who sells his standing grain to be harvested. He sold the grain standing in his field (standing grain) for harvesting.

and even if he hired him to take half the harvest or a third or a quarter as his wage. Even when the worker has a right in the grain while it is still attached to the ground, in which case he is considered the owner of the field and is forbidden to take leket (see below 6:6), his household members are nevertheless permitted to glean after him.
to seat. To settle.
there were poor there who are not eligible to take leket. For example, poor people who have two hundred zuz (see below 9:13).
for the sake of the ways of peace. Similarly see above 1:9, below 7:7.
one who declares leket ownerless. So that the wealthy can also acquire it, and not only the poor.
with the falling of most of it. When most of the stalk has left his hand, or the sickle.
he has no authority over it. And he cannot declare ownerless what is not his.
what is peret?. Mentioned above (1:7) as one of the gifts to the poor in the vineyard.
and it got tangled in leaves and fell to the ground and was detached. The cluster got tangled in the leaves, and because of this it fell and grapes were separated from it.
it is not peret. Similar to the law of leket, above, halachah 2.
he was harvesting and throwing to the ground. And his clusters became mixed with peret.
even half a cluster in which peret was found. And although three grapes are not peret, the Sages penalized him (Radbaz).
the basket. A basket, so that the grapes that are detached during the harvest will fall into it and the poor will not take them.
what is an olelet?. It too was mentioned above (1:7) as one of the gifts to the poor in the vineyard.

a shoulder, small branches attached to the stalk one on top of the other. The stalk is the central branch of the cluster on which the grapes hang. A shoulder means small clusters (branches) that extend from the stalk of the cluster and are piled on its sides.
a nataf, grapes attached to the stalk and descending. Grapes that grow along the stalk and cover it to its end.
and provided that all the grapes of the olelot touch the palm of his hand. That the cluster is not thick, so that if placed on a flat surface, all the grapes touch it.
like an infant to an adult. Like a baby in relation to a grown person.
and a single berry. A cluster with only one grape.
and at the joint of the vine shoot, an olelet. In the branch from which the cluster emerges there is a joint from which an olelet also emerges.
cut off. Is cut.
it belongs to the owner of the vineyard. For it turns out to be part of the cluster (similar to the law of leket above, halachah 3).
they are entitled to take peret and olelot. They are permitted to take them.

that yield a revi'it. That a quarter-log of wine can be pressed from them (Rash Sirilio, Jerusalem Talmud, Pe'ah 7:7), and some explain a quarter of a kav of grapes (Melechet Shlomo, Pe'ah 7:7, Pe'at HaShulchan 8:24).
before the olelot were recognizable. Before they were distinguishable.
once the olelot are recognizable, the olelot belong to the poor. For one cannot consecrate what is not his.

and they shall pay the wages of their growth to the Temple treasury. The poor shall pay the Temple treasury for the improvement of the olelot from the consecrated land, from the time of the consecration until they were picked.
and just as one who cuts off the clusters, so one who cuts off the olelot. For through this the vine improves, and the poor will also benefit from this (Jerusalem Talmud, Pe'ah 7:4).
a gentile who sold his vineyard to an Israelite to harvest. He sold him the right to harvest the vineyard, without a right in the land.
tevel tithe. First tithe given to the Levite from which the terumah of the tithe, to be given to the kohen, has not yet been separated.
he gives them to the poor. For we assume that this is an olelet that had to be given to the poor.
and if it is cut with the cluster etc.. If it is attached by the same vine shoot to the cluster, it belongs to the owner as above, halachah 20, and he may therefore give it to the Levite as tithe.

he may make it terumat ma'aser. The Levite may use this olelet for any purpose, even as terumat ma'aser (and we are not concerned that the olelet was a poor person's and therefore exempt from tithes and cannot serve as terumat ma'aser).
for another place. For terumat ma'aser may be separated also for produce that is not in the place where it is separated (Hilchot Terumot 3:20).

if to eat them as grapes, he is exempt from peret etc.. Generally the harvest of a vineyard is for making wine in the winepress, and therefore the harvest here is a casual harvest and is exempt from the gifts to the poor (Aruch HaShulchan 13:16, and see above 2:6).
the fourth-year fruit. The Torah's commandment to eat the fruit in the fourth year after planting in holiness in Jerusalem, like second tithe (see Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni VeNeta Revai 9:1).
and it is obligated in olelot. For the obligation of olelot does not depend on harvesting, but the poor acquire them from the time they become recognizable (as above, halachah 23).
and if he harvested them to drink as wine, he is obligated in everything. For it looks like a fixed harvest.
unless he left some of them. That he did not harvest them, in which case it does not look like a fixed harvest.
a hidden sheaf. That he covered with dirt or something else, and finally forgot it.
I know that the workers forget the sheaf in such-and-such place. But the owner himself remembers them.
and they forgot it. Eventually the sheaf was forgotten both by the owner and by the workers.
and if it was in the field... it is not forgotten. Since he remembered the sheaf initially, forgetting no longer applies to it.
for what is forgotten from the beginning. That from beginning to end the sheaf was forgotten.

"and you forget a sheaf in the field" - not in the city. The laws of forgetting and remembering concern one who is in the field, and therefore when the owner is in the city, the fact that he remembered the sheaf initially does not remove it from the law of forgotten sheaves.
the poor stood in front of it. They hid the sheaf with their bodies.

or covered it with straw and he remembers the straw. Only if he remembers the straw, for if he forgot the straw it can be assumed that he would have forgotten the sheaf even if it had not been hidden in straw (Aruch HaShulchan 9:10, Yad Peshutah), and in these cases the poor were penalized for their actions so that it is not considered forgetting (Rosh, Pe'ah 5:7, Yad Peshutah).

or he took hold of it to carry it to the city and left it in the field and forgot it, it is not forgotten. Since the sheaves had already reached their final collection point before being moved to the city, and after this there is no more forgetting (as below, halachah 12 - Yad Peshutah, Commentary on the Mishnah, Pixler edition; for a different explanation see Mishneh LeMelech and Derech Emunah).
but if he took it from place to place... it is forgotten. Since he is still moving the sheaves within the field, they have not reached their final collection point.
next to the gate. Next to the gate of the field.
or to the stack. To the pile of sheaves.
it is forgotten. Even though the sheaf was found near certain places, we do not say that he remembered it.

if he remembered the upper one before he came upon it etc.. If he remembered on his own to take the upper sheaf before he saw it, the lower one is not forgotten, for when he comes to take the upper one he will take the lower one with it (Pe'at HaShulchan 9:9). In any case the upper one is not forgotten, since he took hold of it to carry it to the city (as in the previous halachah).
and forgot the fourth. And already passed it (Aruch HaShulchan 11:11), for only when he forgot the sheaf and passed it is it forgotten, as below, halachah 10.

if there was a sixth etc.. Since three sheaves remain, they form an independent row, and the fourth is part of it. It is not forgotten until he takes the fifth, since the sheaves of the row can also be gathered in reverse order: sixth, fifth, and fourth (Aruch HaShulchan, there).

and if there were only five etc.. The two sheaves that remain do not form a row, and therefore the fourth is considered forgotten immediately once he passed it and delayed for the time it takes to take it.
a field whose sheaves are scattered. Not arranged in rows.
it is not forgotten until he takes all around it. Since he can gather the sheaves from several directions, it is not considered that he passed it.

even though they are buried in the ground... one who harvests at night... and likewise a blind person who forgot, they have forgotten sheaves. Even when the forgetting resulted from various factors, it is considered forgetting (Yad Peshutah).
he intends to take only the large ones. If he intended to take only the large sheaves.
for anyone who stipulates against what is written in the Torah, his stipulation is void. As in Hilchot Ishut 6:9-10, and other places.

before it was fully grown, to feed it to an animal. While it is soft, to feed an animal. And it is exempt because it is not customary to make sheaves for animals, and forgetting applies only to sheaves, as it says "and you forget a sheaf in the field" (Rash Sirilio, Pe'ah 6:7).
and likewise if he harvested it in small bundles. Exempt, because he did not make sheaves of the usual size (according to Commentary on the Mishnah, Pe'ah 6:10).

and likewise garlic and onions that he pulled in small bundles to be sold in the market etc.. This refers to a case where he picked some of them to sell right away, and there is no forgetting here since he left the others intentionally (Yad Peshutah).
to make a threshing floor of them. To gather them in a pile.
and forgot in front of him. He left the last sheaf in the row and moved on to the next row.
and behind him. He skipped one of the sheaves.
and they forgot in front of them. For example, they skipped a sheaf or forgot the last sheaf in the row.
and behind them. When they began the harvest, a sheaf that was not harvested remained behind both of them.

because each of them, what is in front of him is behind his fellow. And it is subject to "you shall not return to take it," as in the previous halachah. And the two harvesters are considered as one person since they are jointly responsible for harvesting the field (Kesef Mishneh).
because it is mixed with the rows from east to west etc.. For the field can also be harvested from east to west, and in this way the harvester had not yet passed this sheaf.
that they cleared to the threshing floor. To the place where the sheaves are collected.
in the middle between behind them. Behind both of them.
and bound them into bundles. Gathered the grain into sheaves.
to a place that is the completion of work. As explained in the next halachah.
to the threshing floor. The grain storage place.

if he cleared the sheaves to a place that is not the completion of work and forgot, he has no forgotten sheaf. For from Scripture they learned that the commandment of forgotten sheaves applies only to the final binding, after which there is no further binding (Commentary on the Mishnah).
to the place of a stack that is the threshing floor. To the place where he will store the sheaves in a pile.
to make of them large bundles. To gather several small sheaves into one larger sheaf.
bundles. Bunches of stalks (smaller than sheaves).
piles of olives and carobs. Small heaps.
bunches of flax. Bundles of flax containing seed (Commentary on the Mishnah, Pe'ah 6:5).
vines. Grapevines.
two that are separate from one another. That do not grow from one root.
and one for the convert. A poor righteous convert (see above 1:9).
of a kav each. Each of them with a volume of a kav.
more than four is not forgotten. Since it is more than four times larger than the other sheaves, it is important and noticeable (compare below, halachah 24).
and not a stack. A pile of grain.
standing grain. Grain that has not been harvested.
one looks at the stalks etc.. Since what is attached to the ground can still grow (Rash Sirilio, Jerusalem Talmud, Pe'ah 6:6).
healthy. Thick.
the scorched. Dried and shriveled.
full. Plump.
beside standing grain that is not forgotten. Next to grain that he intends to harvest.
a stalk. A stem.
even if it contained two se'ah. In which case even if it was forgotten, it is not forgotten (above, halachah 18).
the shafkhani. Because it produces a lot of oil (from the word meaning "pour").
the beshani. Because it produces little oil (from the word meaning "shame").
one of these three things. Known by its location, by its deeds, or by its name.
it was designated in his mind. The tree was special in the eyes of the owner of the field.
it is like famous and known. And is not forgotten.
the date palm designates it. Makes it special in its place.

this one designates that one. Although seemingly each of them alone is not designated in the mind of the owner of the field, since there is another like it, they are not forgotten, because two netofah olive trees next to each other are not a common thing (Yad Peshutah; for other interpretations see Radbaz, Aruch HaShulchan 12:8, and Derech Emunah).
that he did not begin. To pick its fruit.
but two se'ah is not forgotten. Similar to the forgotten sheaf, above, halachah 18.
as we have explained. Above, halachah 22.
and why did they say only regarding the olive?. For forgetting can occur in such a case with all trees.
because it was important there in the Land of Israel at that time. For the emperor Hadrian destroyed the Land and cut down its olive trees (Jerusalem Talmud, Pe'ah 7:1).
in an arisa. A vineyard of trellised vines.
whoever cannot stretch out his hand and take it. If he moved on and his hand cannot reach the vine he forgot.
and in a vineyard. Whose vines are spread on the ground.
in a trellised vine. A vine trained upward on something high.
it is not forgotten until he harvests all around it. For as long as he is harvesting around it, he is accustomed to check that he did not forget any of the trees he already harvested.
he is exempt from everything. From all gifts to the poor, as stated above 2:2.
as will be explained. Hilchot Terumot 2:11-12.
a sixth. In addition to leket, forgotten sheaves, pe'ah, peret, and olelot, explained in the previous chapters.
from the produce of the land. From the crops of the ground, as opposed to charity, which will be explained below, chapters 7-10.

and its work is finished. The final action in the process of working the crop is called "completion of work," and from then it is obligated in tithes (Hilchot Ma'aser 3:1, and see there 8-13 for the definition of completion of work for each kind).
and it belongs to its owners, who eat it in Jerusalem. Unlike the other tithes, which are given to others.
the Sabbatical cycle. Seven years at whose end is the Sabbatical year are called a "shavua."

all of it is ownerless. The owner of the field must declare ownerless everything that grows in this year (Hilchot Shemitah 4:24), and ownerless produce is exempt from terumot and ma'aserot (Hilchot Terumot 2:11).

and outside the Land, where there is no Sabbatical year for the land etc.. There is no commandment to declare the field ownerless (Hilchot Shemitah 4:25). And although outside the Land is exempt from terumot and ma'aserot by Torah law, the Sages ordained tithing in the lands adjacent to the Land of Israel (Hilchot Terumot 1:1).

they rely on it in the seventh year. In the Sabbatical year they may go there to receive the poor tithe, since these lands are near the Land of Israel (there; for this principle see also there 1:5, and Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 1:14).
in the land of Shinar. Babylonia.

in the order of most years. Like most years, in which they separate second tithe. The Sages did not ordain separating the poor tithe there, since Babylonia is farther from the Land of Israel (Radbaz).
"and to the Levites you shall speak". And the continuation of the verse: "when you take from the children of Israel the tithe... you shall raise from it a portion for the Lord, a tithe of the tithe."
that the poor passed over. While it was in the field (below, halachah 12).
from half a kav. The amount of baking bread to eat for a whole day, for the morning meal and the evening meal (and likewise for other kinds, the measure is enough to eat or drink for a whole day).
spelt. One of the grain species.
dried figs. Separate dried figs.
fig cake. Dried figs pressed into one mass.
not less than the weight of twenty-five sela. About 420 grams. Fig cake and vegetables were sold by weight, and the other kinds by volume (Derech Emunah, based on Rashi and Rash).
from half a log. So that he can drink a revi'it in the morning and a revi'it in the evening.
from a revi'it. A quarter of a log (about 75 cc), enough to accompany the bread he will eat during the day.
a quarter of a kav. Rice is filling even in a small quantity.
he gives the weight of a litra. About half a log (Hilchot Eruvin 1:12).
of nuts, ten. Ten units.
of other fruits. Which are not eaten regularly, unlike the kinds we have listed so far (Shenot Eliyahu, Pe'ah 8:5).
that is distributed at the threshing floor. In the field.
the owners have no benefit of giving. The owners have no right to profit from choosing which poor person they give to (see also above 1:8).
and even a poor person in Israel etc.. Even if the owner of the field is poor, he must give to other poor people (see also above 1:8).
but what is distributed in the house, the owners have benefit of giving. And the owner may receive payment in exchange for giving the tithe to a particular poor person (see Hilchot Terumot 12:20).
to a poor relative or acquaintance. A family member or an acquaintance.
according to the measure we stated. Above, halachah 8.
for he does not find anything there to buy. The poor person finds no food in the field to buy.
a man and a woman came. Poor people, to take poor tithe.
one gives to the woman first. For her shame is greater than his, since it is not her way to go from door to door (see below 8:15).
two partners. In money, but not in this field (Derech Emunah).
who took a field as sharecroppers. To work the field in exchange for a certain percentage of the crop.
from his share. After they harvested the crop and divided it between them.

to take a portion in the whole field. Since the owner of the field gave him a share in the crop already at the time of the harvest, the whole field is considered the harvester's property, and a person may not take gifts to the poor from his own field (as above, halachah 10, and see above 4:11).
he has nothing until he harvests. His share in the grain will be his only after the harvest.

and at the time of harvest he is poor. That is, he is not the owner of the field (Derech Emunah, based on Kehillat Yaakov, Zera'im, no. 3, that the Torah forbade the owner of the field to take gifts from his own field because with regard to it he is considered wealthy).
and he acquired his share that he harvested. And he cannot take poor tithe from his own.
land and produce. Both the body of the land and the produce in it.
he is permitted in leket, forgotten sheaves, pe'ah, and poor tithe of it. Since it is not his.
even though he has not yet paid the money. Rather he acquired by the act of a document or a cloth, the field is entirely his and he is forbidden its gifts.
and even if he borrowed the money and bought it. Even if he acquired by the act of money with borrowed funds, the field is considered the buyer's.
poor tithe etc.. And similarly with second tithe (Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 3:21), and with the proceeds of Sabbatical-year produce (Hilchot Shemitah 6:10).
one does not repay a loan from it. If the owner of the field owes money to a poor person, he cannot give him poor tithe in payment of his debt.

and one does not pay back favors from it. If the poor person did him a favor in the past, the owner of the field cannot give him poor tithe money as an expression of gratitude, for this too is like repaying a debt (Beit Yosef, Yoreh De'ah 231).

and one does not make a shoshvinut gift from it. Money that used to be given to a groom to help with his wedding needs (the details are explained in Hilchot Zechiyah UMatanah, chapter 7). And it is forbidden to give it from poor tithe, because if the recipient does not return it to the giver when the giver marries, the giver can claim it in court, and therefore giving a shoshvinut gift is considered a loan or a transaction (Tosefta Kifshutah, Pe'ah p. 189, Derech Emunah).
and one does not give anything from it for charity. If the charity collectors assessed him a certain amount to contribute, this would be like paying a debt (Beit Yosef, there).
an act of kindness. Doing a favor for his fellow that he is not obligated to do.

and he must inform him that it is poor tithe. So that the recipient will know that he need not feel gratitude to him; otherwise this is a forbidden use of poor tithe, resembling a transaction (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Demai 4:4).

and one gives it to the city chaver with goodwill. A chaver of the city is a Torah scholar living in the city (Commentary on the Mishnah, Berachot 4:7), who also serves as a charity collector (as below 7:14). And it is permitted to give him poor tithe in order that he distribute it to charity, even in a way that the city chaver feels gratitude to him for it (according to Derech Emunah).
"and you shall leave it in your gates". "In your gates" - this is the Land of Israel.
according to what is fitting for the poor person. To make up for his lack, as in the next halachah 3.
if the giver's hand is able. If his financial situation permits.

"and you shall strengthen him". Even an interest-free loan is considered an excellent form of giving and even preferable to charity (see below 10:7, Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 1:1, Ahavat Chesed part 1, 1:1).
and you shall not shut. Do not close.
they clothe him. They give him clothing.
and a servant running before him. In order to honor him.
that he lacks. According to what this poor person lacks.
and they spread a bed for him. They give him a bed and bedding.
and all his household utensils. Household items according to the custom of his place (Derech Emunah; for example, in our day, electrical appliances and furniture - Ahavat Tzedakah 6:4).
and afterward they marry him to a wife. For this is the proper order: to marry a wife after one has a home (Hilchot De'ot 5:11).
according to the ability of his hand. According to the giver's means.
a fifth. A fifth.
an evil eye. Stinginess.

and a person should never withhold himself from giving a third of a shekel a year. The minimum amount to fulfill the commandment of charity is the value of pure silver weighing a third of a shekel, once a year (the measure of a third of a shekel is about 6.5 grams of silver according to the accepted view).
they sustain him immediately. Since hunger is great suffering (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 9a).
naked. Dressed in wretched clothing (Yad Ramah and Ritva there).
and if they knew him. That he is poor and does not deceive, and they know what his needs are according to his station (see below, halachah 8).
and they do not investigate him. Lest he does not need so much or is now deceiving (Rik"v; see there and Derech Emunah, who brought further explanations).
with the poor of Israel for the sake of the ways of peace. See also above 1:9, Hilchot Melachim 10:12.
one does not attend to him with a large gift. Since by going door to door he collects from many people.
a dried fig. A dry fig.
a bed on which to sleep etc.. A bed and bedding.
and if he stayed for Shabbat. He remained in the city over Shabbat.
to a poor person who passes from place to place. Who is not from the town, and needs food for that day.

from one loaf sold for a pundion etc.. A loaf of bread whose price is half a ma'ah (a "pundion"), when four se'ah of flour sell for twenty-four ma'ot (a "sela"). Such a loaf contains about a quarter of a kav (about 300 cc) of flour, and is enough for eating two meals (Commentary on the Mishnah, Pe'ah 8:7, Eruvin 8:2).
and we have already explained all the measures. The volume measures in Hilchot Eruvin 1:12-13, and the coins in Hilchot Shekalim 1:2-4.
and if he lodged. Slept the night in the town.
as a gift. In a respectful way, so that he will think that the gift is not from charity funds (Tur, Yoreh De'ah 253:9).
they do not pay attention to him. They do not concern themselves with him.
what they estimated him to give. What the court assesses that he can give.
and they go down to his property etc.. They take some of his belongings and sell them.
and they take pledges for charity. They take a pledge that will be returned only after he donates properly.
even on Fridays. When people are busy.
a spendthrift. A wastrel.
who pinches himself. Lives in financial straits.
who shames him. Who embarrasses him.
He will in the future exact payment from him. The Holy One, blessed be He.

one does not assess charity on orphans. One does not collect charity from the money of minor orphans, since they are educated only in commandments with a fixed measure and clear limit, such as tzitzit and lulav (Hilchot Nachalot 11:10).
even for the redemption of captives. Which is an exceedingly important commandment (below 8:10).
in order to make a name for themselves. To publicize their generosity for their own benefit.
charity collectors. And likewise the poor person himself.
and from children. From minors.

for the presumption of a large amount is theft or robbery from others. For if they donate a large sum, it should be assumed that this was done without the owner's knowledge, or that they stole from another person (and see also Hilchot Genevah 6:4).
his relative. A member of his family.
and the poor of his household. His neighbors (Rema, Yoreh De'ah 251:3).
one who went on a business trip. Traveled to another city for business and stayed there.
and they assessed him etc.. They imposed on him to give charity (see below 9:12).
he gives to the poor of that city. For the individual is drawn after the people of the city and must act as they do.
they give. To the city's collectors, so that they will not be suspected of not giving charity.
and when they come etc.. When they return to their city, they take back the money and give it to the poor of their own city.
and if there is a city chaver there. If in the city to which they came there is a Torah scholar who handles the distribution of charity (see above 6:17).
one who says etc.. And it is not possible to ask him which synagogue he intended to donate to.
that he is accustomed to. Where he generally prays.
they shall be given to both. They shall divide it between them.
charity is included among vows. When he accepted upon himself to give charity, it is like a vow of consecration (see Hilchot Nedarim 1:2).

you shall not delay paying it. The prohibition of delaying the bringing of offerings that a person obligated himself to give (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 14:13), which also includes the prohibition of delaying charity he committed to.
who vowed charity. Who said: "I hereby owe a sela for charity."
or pledged it. Who said: "This sela is for charity" (Hilchot Nedarim 1:2).
to change it and refine it into gold. For example, to exchange several silver coins for a gold coin.
these are permitted. But if he did not stipulate at the time of the vow or pledge, he may not change it (below, halachah 4).
one who attaches to charity. One who causes a charity vow he made regarding a specific item to apply also to another item (see also Hilchot Nedarim 3:3-5).
one who says, "this sela is like that one". One who says of his own coin that it should be like a charity coin.
he must give until he says, "this is not what I intended". For a similar law see Hilchot Arachin VaCharamin 2:8.
to change it for another. To exchange it for a different coin.
but once it reached the hand of the collector, it is forbidden to change it. For the poor have already acquired it.
to combine the coins and make them into denarii. To exchange many small coins for a few denarii (for each denar is worth six ma'ot).
they combine for others. They give another person charity coins, and he gives denarii.

but not for themselves. It is forbidden to exchange for the collector's own denarii, so that they not be suspected of misappropriating charity funds (this law is also brought below 9:11 among the things forbidden to collectors because of suspicion).

if the poor had benefit etc.. If the poor profit from the collector borrowing the money for his private needs, for example the collector tells people that there is no money in the fund and thus causes them to donate, he is permitted to borrow (Babylonian Talmud, Arachin 6b and Rashi there. But if he did not borrow the money, he may not say a falsehood and claim that there is no money in the fund - Radbaz).
like consecrated property. Like something consecrated to the Temple.

it is forbidden to change it, but if for a matter of a mitzvah, it is permitted to change it. The community may not sell the lamp and buy with the proceeds something optional for the community's use, since the donor gave it for a mitzvah purpose, and it may not be changed to an optional use without his consent (Derech Emunah).
was forgotten. Was no longer remembered.

and if the owner's name was forgotten from it etc.. If it is no longer called by his name, it is like all communal property, which the community may change even to an optional purpose (see also below 9:7).
lest the gentile say etc.. And this would be a desecration of God's name.
for themselves. For their own needs.
for the upkeep of the Temple. For the Temple's property.
they do not accept from him initially. In the first instance.

they do not return to him. But the donation is not used for the Temple's upkeep, as learned from the verses later in this halachah; rather the court decides what to do with it (see Hilchot Arachin VaCharamin 1:11-12).
and if it was a specific item. That can be identified even when part of a building.
they return it to him so that they will not have a specific item in the Temple. And it is not possible to make other use of the donation as explained above, halachah 7.

not for you and us. The continuation of the verse: "to build a house for our God." So the returnees from Babylon said to their gentile neighbors when they offered to partner in building the Temple, and from here we learn that one does not accept at all from a gentile a donation for the building of the Temple (see also Hilchot Shekalim 4:8, Hilchot Arachin VaCharamin there).
I separated it with the knowledge of Israel. His intention was that they decide what to do with this money.
perhaps in his heart it is for Heaven. To consecrate to the Temple.

it is forbidden for an Israelite to take charity from gentiles publicly. Because he demeans himself (Hilchot Edut 11:5), and there is a desecration of God's name in that the gentiles say that Jews do not support their poor (Levush, Yoreh De'ah 254:1).
for the sake of the peace of the kingdom. So as not to disturb peace with the king.
you shall not stand by the blood of your neighbor. The prohibition of being negligent in saving an Israelite in danger (Hilchot Rotze'ach 1:14).
he shall not rule over him with rigor in your sight. The prohibition of allowing a gentile to subject an Israelite to hard labor (Hilchot Avadim 1:6).
they spend the money on it. They use the money for the commandment.
and they scraped the stones. They hewed them.
and split the beams. They sawed them into pieces.

they should not sell the synagogue, but collect from the public for their redemption. For a person in need of money does not sell his house (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 3b), but does everything he can to obtain money in another way.
for more than their value. At a price higher than the accepted one.
so that the enemies will not pursue them to capture them. So as not to encourage gentiles to take more Jews captive.
they make the yoke heavy on them. They make the conditions of imprisonment harsher and torture them (Commentary on the Mishnah, Gittin 4:6).
or borrowed from them. And did not return the money.
it is a commandment to redeem him. This commandment rests upon his relatives, and if they cannot, upon all of Israel (Hilchot Avadim 2:7).
a third time, they do not redeem him. Because it is evident that he does this so that they will redeem him.

but they redeem the sons after the death of their father. So that they not assimilate among the gentiles; during their father's life there is no such concern, since their father guards them (Rashi, Gittin 47a).

a slave who was captured etc.. A Canaanite slave who was sold to an Israelite and accepted upon himself the commandments that slaves are obligated in, is in an intermediate status between a gentile and an Israelite (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 12:11).
eats carrion to spite. Not for pleasure, for example when kosher meat is also before him, and he eats specifically the forbidden (Babylonian Talmud, Gittin 47a).
it is forbidden to redeem him. See also Hilchot Rotze'ach 4:10.
to go from door to door. To go from door to door.
because it is not his way. Of homosexual relations.
six denarii and a quarter denar of pure silver. About 26 grams of pure silver. This sum is enough to buy simple clothes for a year (Hilchot Ishut 13:1).
from the charity fund. From the public fund.

to a challal. Whose mother had relations with a kohen in a forbidden union (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 19:3). The reason an Israelite takes precedence over him is that a daughter of a challal is unfit for the priesthood, while a daughter of an Israelite is fit for the priesthood (Commentary on the Mishnah, Horayot 3:8).
to a shetuki. Whose father is not known, and who is a possible mamzer (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 15:12).
to an asufi. Who was picked up from the marketplace and whose parents are not known, and who is a possible mamzer (there, halachah 13).
to a mamzer. Who was born from forbidden relations (there, halachah 1).
to a natin. A descendant of the Gibeonites who converted, called netinim because Joshua gave them to be woodcutters and water drawers (there 12:22-23).
for the natin grew up with us in holiness. He was born as an Israelite.
to a freed slave. A Canaanite slave who was freed, whose law is like that of a convert (there 13:12).
because he was included in the curse. "Cursed be Canaan; a servant of servants shall he be to his brothers" (Genesis 9:25).

and if one of them was his teacher etc.. When a person redeems with his private funds, he gives precedence to his teacher or his father (and regarding precedence between his father and his teacher, see Hilchot Talmud Torah 5:1).
they go around to the people from Friday to Friday. They go from house to house every Friday.
and a fixed amount upon him. The sum he must give according to his financial ability.
on the spot. Occasionally.
tamchui. A vessel in which food is given (Commentary on the Mishnah, Pe'ah 8:7), after which the method of distribution described in our halachah is named.
on fast days they distribute food to the poor. At the end of the fast.
and lodged. Went to sleep.

if they did not distribute the bread and the fruit eaten with the bread. Fruit eaten together with bread, for the bread and fruit are ready to eat and the poor rely on receiving them at the end of the fast.
the fund is collected only by two. Two collectors go around together to collect for the fund.
authority over the public in monetary matters. Collection of money that involves coercion, since pledges are taken for charity as above 7:10.

and it is permitted to trust one with the money of the fund. For the need for two is not because of trustworthiness but because of authority, and therefore after they collected the money it may be deposited with one treasurer.
as in monetary cases. Which are judged by three judges (Hilchot Sanhedrin 5:8).
that he gives each one enough for his needs for Shabbat. Food sufficient for seven days as above, halachah 1, and it is necessary to deliberate and decide how much to give each poor person.
for it is not a fixed amount. And they must deliberate how much to collect from each person.

and the tamchui is for the poor of the world. For poor people who come to the city from other places (who are given food for two meals as above 7:8), since the poor of the city already received from the fund for the whole week (and if nevertheless one of the city's poor lacks, he is given from the tamchui - Derech Emunah).

to make the fund a tamchui. To transfer to the tamchui a donation given to the fund, for example where there are many transient poor and few resident poor (Tur, Yoreh De'ah 256), since donors are not particular about this, but give with the understanding that the community leaders may change it (Beit Yosef, there).
they may not separate from one another in the marketplace. For they collect only in pairs as above, halachah 5, and if they separate from each other they may arouse suspicion of embezzlement.

but so that there will be etc.. They are permitted to separate only briefly, in a way that one goes to collect in a shop and the other goes to collect at the gate in front of the shop, and they can see each other (Tur and Rema 257:1).
he may not put them into his pocket. Because of suspicion.
who has a claim against his fellow for a maneh. Who demands from his fellow a debt of a hundred denarii.

and you shall be clean before the Lord and before Israel. Just as one must be clean and upright toward the Holy One, blessed be He, who knows everything, so one must be clean in the eyes of people and avoid a situation that arouses suspicion.
they combine the coins etc.. See above 8:4 for explanation.
they sell to others. The foods in the tamchui.

and one does not audit the charity collectors. To know how much they collected and how much they distributed; rather they are trusted, since only trustworthy people are appointed as collectors, as above, halachah 1.
consecrated property. Money consecrated to the Temple.
in the province. In the city.

thirty days, they compel him to give charity to the fund. For a donation to the fund is the most basic donation, on which the poor of the city depend (Responsa Maharik 17, brought by Kesef Mishneh, halachah 6).
a merchant. A trader.
and they are a debt upon him. He owes this sum to another person.

pledged for his wife's ketubah. That they agreed between them that the wife would collect her ketubah from this money if the husband dies or divorces her (Shach and Taz on Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh De'ah 253:1).
who needed. Who needed to receive charity, for example because he does not have two hundred zuz.
vessels for eating and drinking, bedding, clothing, and the like. For with such items it is repugnant for a person to use a lower grade than he is accustomed to.
such as a scraper. Used for scratching the body (Rif, Ketubot 29b).
a pestle. A pounding implement.
and buys less than them. Buys vessels made of cheaper material.

in what case does this apply? Before he reaches the point of collecting from the people etc.. When he needs charity temporarily, he need not sell expensive eating and drinking vessels, but once he has become like one of the poor and wants to receive charity from the public fund on a regular basis, he may not live at the public's expense before selling all his expensive vessels (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Pe'ah 8:8 and Yad Peshutah).
one who had houses etc.. This halachah deals with a person who has no money for sustenance but has land he can sell.

they feed him poor tithe up to half their value etc.. They give him poor tithe or charity to cover the loss if he sells in winter, which is at most half the property's value (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Kama 7b). However, they do not give him the amount all at once, but give him daily sustenance each day (Beit Yosef, Yoreh De'ah 253:3), and he may do as he wishes - either wait until summer or sell in winter and thus not lose (Sefer HaEshkol, Hilchot Tzedakah p. 215).
if others were selling at a high price etc.. If the time is suitable for selling, but he cannot sell at the proper price because people know that he is pressed to sell.
and they collected a surplus. They collected more.
the surplus is his. Since the donors donated for him, the entire sum is acquired by him (Responsa of the Rosh 32:6).

and the surplus of the poor is for the poor etc.. If they collected for the poor in general and did not distribute everything, they keep the remainder until other poor people come. Likewise if they collected for redeeming captives or for burying the dead and did not use the entire sum.
the surplus of a captive is for that captive. If he was freed using part of the money collected, they give him the rest of the money (for the same reason explained regarding a poor person).
worn-out garments. Worn and tattered clothes.
for I have known him, so that he will command. The continuation of the verse: "his children and his household after him, that they keep the way of the Lord, to do righteousness and justice."
the throne of Israel. The kingdom of Israel.
is established. Is based.
and those who return to her through righteousness. The exiles from Zion will return to it through charity.
became poor. Became poor.
was brought about. Was caused.
for cruelty is found only among the gentiles. See also Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 19:17.
and the one who is joined to them. The converts.
base. Without the yoke of Heaven's kingship (Rashi, Deuteronomy 13:14).

as it says, "You hear the cry of the poor". There is no such verse in Scripture; the citation here is from the liturgical poem "Nishmat Kol Chai," according to the Sephardic text (although this passage does not appear in the text of the prayers in the Rambam's order of prayers at the end of Sefer Ahavah).
from their cry. From their prayer to the Creator of the world.
for a covenant has been made with them. It is promised to them that their prayer will be accepted.

he destroyed his merit or lost it. If he gave in anger he completely lost his merit, and if he gave with sorrow he lost part of his merit but did not lose it completely, as below, halachah 14 (Shach, Yoreh De'ah 249:9).
and causes them to do. Causes them to do.

his reward is greater than the reward of the giver. For he brings merit to both the giver and the recipient, and also because in collecting charity from others one encounters humiliations and insults that are more painful than spending money.
and those who bring the many to righteousness are like the stars. Those who cause many to be righteous are considered to shine like stars.

one who strengthens an Israelite who has fallen. One who helps an Israelite whose financial condition is declining and prevents him from reaching financial collapse. This kind of giving is the finest, since its effects are long term and the recipient is not so embarrassed (and see Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 1:1).
and gives him a gift. The way friends give gifts to one another, since the recipient is not yet poor and therefore is not so embarrassed.
finds him work. Finds him a job or employs him.
the chamber of secrets. A chamber that operated in secrecy and concealment.
those of good families. From honorable families who are ashamed to receive charity.

and close to this is one who gives into a charity fund. For here too the giver and recipient do not know about one another, but in any case it is not like the chamber of secrets since the collector or the public sees that he donated to the fund (Rik"v).
like Chananiah ben Teradyon. Who was a charity collector (see Babylonian Talmud, Avodah Zarah 17b and the commentators there).
they bundle the coins. They tie together a quantity of coins.
and throw them behind them. They hang them behind their backs.
before he asks. Before he requests.
through righteousness I shall behold Your face. Through charity I will merit the revelation of God's face in prayer.

his adult sons and daughters whom he is not obligated to feed. From age six and up, when he must feed them by rabbinic enactment, though he is not compelled to (Rik"v and Kesef Mishneh, based on Hilchot Ishut 12:14-15). Some explain that this refers to truly grown children whom he is not obligated to feed even by rabbinic enactment (Derech Emunah, Yad Peshutah).
for the relative comes first. As above 7:13.
and delights in Him. Delights in God (as stated in the continuation of the verses: "then you shall delight in the Lord" - Isaiah 58:14).
the seed of Ham. The descendants of Ham son of Noah, of whom it is said, "a servant of servants shall he be to his brothers" (Genesis 9:25).
every day he adds sin and iniquity to the world. For slaves are accustomed to robbing (Mishnah Avot 2:7).
and be dragged along in distress. Conduct his life in great austerity.
make your Shabbat like a weekday. Eat weekday foods on Shabbat.
and did not accept from them when they gave to them. They did not agree to accept financial help even when people wanted to give voluntarily.
and out of arrogance does not take. Is unwilling to accept help because of his self-importance.
this is a shedder of blood and is liable for his life. If he dies or becomes more ill as a result.
and he has nothing from his suffering but iniquities and sins. For he thinks he is performing commandments and piety, but it is nothing but sin and guilt - not a mitzvah (Rik"v).
and pressed the hour. Exerted himself to sustain himself at that time.
